title: The overrepresented and the underestimated. September 14, 2026.
excerpt: From a language compromise that took three years to negotiate, to a cobbler's son now employing 4,500 people, September 14's five stories are about people and institutions doing more than their starting position suggested they could.
bodyHtml:
Some days this project's five stories share a thread by coincidence. September 14 is one of them: every story here is about someone or something exceeding what their starting conditions predicted.

The compromise that had to work

On September 14, 1949, after nearly three years of debate, India's Constituent Assembly adopted Hindi in Devanagari script as the Union's official language - Article 343 of the Constitution, reached through what's known as the Munshi-Ayyangar formula. A country with hundreds of languages doesn't arrive at one official choice by accident or by simple majority vote; it takes genuine, sustained negotiation to protect every other language's status while still settling on one for official business. Nearly 77 years later, India still marks the date every year as Hindi Diwas.

A target hit five years early

India's clean energy story this year is almost the opposite of a headline-grabbing announcement - it's a target quietly beaten well ahead of schedule. As of June 2025, more than 50% of India's installed electricity capacity comes from non-fossil sources, a milestone that wasn't due under India's Paris Agreement commitment until 2030. This past financial year alone added a record 55.3 GW of non-fossil capacity, the most ever added in a single year, bringing the total past 283 GW. Climate targets usually get missed or hit right at the wire; beating one by five years means the underlying build-out was moving faster than the target itself.

From a cobbler's son to 4,500 employees

Ashok Khade's story starts about as far from a corporate boardroom as it's possible to get: the son of a cobbler in rural Maharashtra, apprenticing as a draftsman at Mazagon Dock before working on a submarine engineering project in West Germany. He came home and co-founded DAS Offshore Engineering with his brothers in the early-to-mid 1990s - a company that now employs over 4,500 people. In 2026, he was awarded the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honors. The starting point doesn't set the ceiling; it just sets how far someone has to travel to get there.

The first in 131 offices, 93 countries

Devika Bulchandani's first came in a different arena entirely. In September 2022, after 26 years at McCann, she was named Global CEO of Ogilvy - the storied British-founded advertising network spanning 131 offices in 93 countries - becoming the first woman of color to lead the agency, and joining an expanding list of Indian-origin executives leading global companies. Indian-origin leadership at the top of global business used to cluster almost entirely in tech and finance; advertising, media, and culture-facing industries are increasingly part of the same story now.

Sixteen companies, five percent of a list

And the pattern shows up at scale, too: per the most recent Fortune 500 analysis (Indiaspora, with Boston Consulting Group, 2024), sixteen Fortune 500 companies are run by Indian-origin CEOs - about 3% of the list's leadership - generating a combined $978 billion in revenue, roughly 5% of total Fortune 500 revenue. That's genuine overrepresentation: a bigger share of revenue than the corresponding share of CEO seats, spanning industries from tech to healthcare to consumer goods to finance.

Five stories, one thread: a language compromise nobody expected to hold, a climate target nobody expected to beat early, a cobbler's son nobody expected to run a company this size, a first nobody expected in advertising, and a revenue share nobody would guess just by counting names on a CEO list. None of it was inevitable. All of it happened anyway.

coverHeadlines: India just hit a climate target five years ahead of schedule. And it wasn't close.
After three years of debate, one language was chosen to speak for an entire country.
He grew up the son of a cobbler in rural Maharashtra. Today, his company has over 4,500 employees.
She became the first woman of color to lead a 131-office global ad network.
Sixteen Fortune 500 companies are run by Indian-origin CEOs. Together, they generate more revenue than most countries' entire economies.
